questions.problem:
Given the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, 
find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an invertible matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{-1}AP.$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal:  

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=4\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=1$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 
The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows: 

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Whether a Given 2x2 Matrix Is Diagonalizable
questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -3 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-2-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(-3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-1I)\text{x}=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-1I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.

questions.problem: Find matrices $P$ and $D$ such that $PD{P}^{-1}=B,$ where $D$ is a diagonal matrix and $B=[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ -6 & -7\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the diagonalization algorithm.

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & 8 \\ -6 & -7-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(-7-\lambda )-8\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda -15 & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)(\lambda +3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-3.$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-5I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ -6 & -7\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ -6 & -12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ -6 & -12 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 8 \\ -6 & -7\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & 8 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & 8 & 0 \\ -6 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Diagonalizing a 2x2 Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 6 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & a \\ 1 & b\end{aligned}]
$$

Given that $D={P}^{-1}AP,$ find the value of $\frac{a}{b}.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the diagonal matrix $D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$, we deduce that the eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ 

Now, we simply need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=1.$ Computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 6 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 \\ -9 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ -9 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=3,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.problem:
Determine if the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ -4 & -4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0$:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}8-\lambda  & 9 \\ -4 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (8-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )-9\cdot (-4) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -32+36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-2I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 9 \\ -4 & -4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable.
